A cranny is a small, narrow crack or opening in a hard surface. Think of a wall that has developed a thin split in it over time, or a rock face with a tiny gap running through it — that gap, that little crack, is a cranny. It is not a big hole. It is not a wide opening. It is specifically small, tight, and narrow.

Imagine an old stone wall. Over many years, the stone shifts slightly and tiny cracks form. Some of these cracks are so narrow you can barely fit a finger in them. Those are crannies. Now imagine a cliff face by the sea, with small gaps and splits running through the rock where wind and water have worn the surface away. Those splits are crannies too.

A cranny is always:

  • Small — not a gaping hole, not a large gap, but a tight, minor crack
  • Narrow — more of a thin slit than a round hole
  • In something solid — a wall, a rock, a cliff, stonework, or similar hard material

A cranny carries a sense of something hidden and hard to reach. Because crannies are so tiny and tucked away, they are the kinds of places where small things disappear — dust, insects, coins, seeds. A spider might make its home in a cranny. A small plant might grow out of one. If you lose a tiny object near an old stone wall, it might fall into a cranny and be nearly impossible to retrieve.

This is why the word has a quiet, slightly mysterious feeling to it — crannies are the overlooked, forgotten little gaps that exist in old and worn surfaces.

You will almost certainly encounter the phrase "nooks and crannies" in your reading and listening, because it is very common in English. You need to understand it well.

A nook is a small, sheltered corner or tucked-away space — like the corner of a room, or a small alcove cut into a wall. It is a recess, a little sheltered spot.

A cranny is a narrow crack or split.

Together, "nooks and crannies" means every small, hidden, or hard-to-reach spot — absolutely everywhere, including all the little corners and gaps you might overlook. It is used to emphasise thoroughness.

For example:

  • "She searched every nook and cranny of the house for her missing key." — This means she searched absolutely everywhere, even the most obscure corners and tiny gaps.
  • "Dust had settled in every nook and cranny of the old library." — This means dust was literally everywhere, in all the little corners and cracks.

The phrase is so commonly used together that many people encounter "cranny" almost exclusively in this pairing. But it is equally correct to use "cranny" on its own.

• "A tiny fern had taken root in a cranny of the ancient castle wall."
  • "The lizard disappeared into a cranny between two large boulders."
  • "The old chimney was full of crannies where birds liked to nest."
  • "He wedged the folded note into a cranny in the wall and hoped no one would find it."

It helps to understand the boundaries of the word:

  • A cranny is not a large crack or split. If a wall has split dramatically in two, that is not a cranny — it is simply a crack, a fracture, or a break. Crannies are small by definition.
  • A cranny is not typically used for soft or flexible materials like fabric or skin. You would not say a fold in a blanket is a cranny. The word belongs to hard, solid surfaces.
  • A cranny is not a hole that goes all the way through something. It is more of a surface-level gap or a split that goes partway in, like a crevice you could tuck something into.

If you needed to define it in one sentence: A cranny is a small, narrow crack or crevice in a hard surface, especially in a wall or rock, typically small enough to be overlooked but large enough for small things to hide in.

That is the complete picture of the word. Whether you see it alone or in the phrase "nooks and crannies," you now know exactly what it means and the precise image it is meant to create.
